The present study found that a single subanesthetic bolus of propofol (35-50 mg/kg, i.p.) rapidly ameliorated acute total SD-induced cognitive impairments, with effects observed as early as one hour after administration and persisting for 24 hours in the Y-maze test, whereas the classical hypnotic zolpidem (ZPD, 1.25-5 mg/kg) was ineffective in rescuing cognition. Propofol's cognitive-improving effect was also demonstrated in novel object recognition and object location recognition tasks. Meanwhile, non-invasive sleep monitoring revealed that propofol increased the proportions of medium-to-long duration non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep (64-128 seconds), and reduced the episode numbers of short-duration NREM sleep (0-4, 4-8, and 8-16 seconds) in SD mice. EEG/EMG recordings confirmed that propofol increased total NREM duration by prolonging mean episode duration. In contrast, ZPD failed to reverse NREM sleep fragmentation under either monitoring modality, although it did prolong total NREM sleep duration. Moreover, propofol upregulated the core circadian regulator BMAL1, reduced the levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β and TNF-α), restored the expression of key neuroplasticity-related proteins (BDNF, PSD-95, and SYN), and reversed SD-induced loss of dendritic spines in the hippocampus. Together, these findings suggest that propofol rapidly ameliorates SD-induced cognitive impairments, and that this behavioral rescue is associated with the restoration of sleep stability and attenuation of neuroinflammation.

papers.title: Variables associated with C-reactive protein greater than 10 mg/L in people with current depression: results from a nationally representative sample of U.S. adults.
papers.abstract: C-reactive protein (CRP) concentrations over10 mg/L are often used to exclude subjects from studies on inflammation and depression, based on the idea that these levelsindicateacute illness. However, the broader effects of this practice at the population level, and in depression samples, are not well understood. We analyzed data from the 2021-2023 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), a representative sample of community dwelling individuals in the U.S. (n = 6,064). Analyses focused on adults, aged 20 and older (51.53% female, 60.15% non-Hispanic White) Participants were categorized by CRP levels (≥ 10 mg/L vs. < 10 mg/L) and probable depression (Patient Health Questionnaire-9 ≥ 10). Weighted multinomial regression models examined demographic, behavioral, biological markers, and health conditions predicting CRP elevation, depression, and their co-occurrence. About 7.11% of U.S. adults had CRP levels ≥ 10 mg/L. Of those with probable depression (12.51% of the sample),nearly 10%also had CRP ≥ 10 mg/L,indicatingthat typical exclusion thresholds could omita significant portionof depressed individuals. CRP ≥ 10 mg/L and co-occurring depression was associated with higher BMI, lower socioeconomic status, as well as sleep disturbance. Non-Hispanic Black participants had a higher chance of CRP ≥ 10 mg/L despite similar odds of depression. Excluding individuals with CRP ≥ 10 mg/L may limit the applicability of study results and disproportionately exclude those with greater medical and socioeconomic challenges. Strategies likestratifying byinflammatory burden and using multi-marker inflammatory profiles could preserve diversity and improve the relevance of research to real-world populations.

papers.title: Brain Reorganization Following Psychological Interventions for Chronic Pain: A Systematic Review of Neuroimaging Evidence.
papers.abstract: Psychological interventions are effective for chronic pain, but their neural mechanisms remain unclear. This review synthesized functional magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalography evidence on treatment-related brain changes following psychological interventions in adults with chronic non-cancer pain. Seven databases were searched. Eligible studies included adults aged 18-64 receiving a psychological intervention with both neuroimaging and clinical outcomes. Study quality was assessed with the Effective Public Health Practice Project tool. Heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis, findings were synthesized narratively. Nineteen studies (n = 843) were included: 15 randomized controlled trials, 3 within-subject designs, and 1 pilot non-randomized trial. Interventions were mindfulness-based interventions (n = 6), cognitive behavioral therapy (n = 5), hypnosis (n = 3), neurofeedback (n = 3), and other approaches (n = 2). The anterior insula, anterior cingulate and midcingulate cortex, prefrontal cortex, and primary somatosensory cortex were most consistently implicated. Cognitive behavioral therapy reduced somatosensory-limbic coupling and enhanced prefrontal engagement. Mindfulness showed convergent insular and cingulate involvement. Pain reprocessing therapy showed close alignment between observed neural changes and its proposed mechanism, with reduced affective-evaluative pain activation and increased prefrontal-somatosensory connectivity. Hypnosis dissociated somatosensory from affective pain processing. Brain-behavior correlations linked predominantly to cognitive-affective outcomes, including catastrophizing, self-efficacy, and anxiety rather than pain intensity. Across interventions, convergent findings implicated increased prefrontal engagement and reduced affective-evaluative pain processing, broadly consistent with cognitive-affective modulation of pain. These findings offer neurobiological plausibility for clinical approaches targeting catastrophizing and fear-avoidance, though guiding patient selection would require research linking neural change directly to clinical outcome. PERSPECTIVE: This review identified shared neuroanatomical hubs, including increased prefrontal regulation and reduced affective-evaluative pain processing across cognitive behavioral therapy, mindfulness, hypnosis, and pain reprocessing therapy. These findings provide neurobiological support for established clinical approaches targeting cognitive-affective responses to pain, but do not establish shared causal mechanisms or support patient stratification. TRIAL REGISTRATION: This systematic review was prospectively registered with PROSPERO (registration number: CRD42024623019).

papers.title: Neural correlates of facial recognition in a social wasp.
papers.abstract: In humans and other primates, faces are special visual objects that are encoded by circuits selective to faces. If specialized circuits are the most efficient way to encode and discriminate among similar-looking objects of high relevance, then we expect that analogous circuits should evolve in other taxa with specialized visual individual recognition abilities. Thus, we surveyed the neural responses to visual objects across the brain of a wasp that has independently evolved specialized facial recognition, Polistes fuscatus. We found a localized population of neurons analogous to face cells, which we term "wasp cells," that selectively fire to front-facing wasp images. Some of these wasp cells encode information about facial patterns, which possibly underlie the unique visual recognition abilities of these wasps. These findings demonstrate high-level feature-selective tuning in an invertebrate and suggest that specialized circuits are an adaptive feature for nervous systems requiring complex visual recognition.

papers.title: Association between Z-hypnotic prescription and clinical, cognitive and seizure duration outcomes of electroconvulsive therapy for depression.
papers.abstract: Evidence regarding the impact of Z-hypnotics (including zopiclone and zolpidem) on electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) outcomes is sparse. This study examined the association between Z-hypnotic prescription and clinical and cognitive outcomes following ECT for depression. A retrospective cohort study of 425 adult inpatients with ICD-10 unipolar or bipolar depression who received an acute course of ECT. Z-hypnotic prescription was defined as zopiclone or zolpidem prescription within 24 h before the first ECT session. In line with local policy, Z-hypnotics were routinely withheld the night before ECT. Outcomes were Clinical Global Impression-Improvement (CGI-I) response after final ECT, cognition (assessed using time to reorientation [TRO]), and electroencephalographic (EEG) and motor seizure duration. Response was analysed using conditional logistic regression; repeated outcomes were analysed using mixed-effects models. Of 425 patients, 153 (36.0%) were prescribed Z-hypnotics at baseline. In 1:1 propensity score-matched analyses (n = 153 per group), Z-hypnotic prescription was not associated with CGI-I response (OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.41; p = 0.508) or motor seizure duration (mean difference, -2.08 s; 95% CI -4.23 to 0.08; p = 0.059). Z-hypnotic prescription was associated with faster TRO (mean difference, -1.85 min; 95% CI -3.30 to -0.41; p = 0.012) and shorter EEG seizure duration (mean difference, -3.15 s; 95% CI -6.09 to -0.21; p = 0.036). Sensitivity analyses were consistent with primary analyses. In a service where Z-hypnotics were routinely withheld the night before ECT, Z-hypnotics were not associated with reduced response, despite small TRO and EEG differences observed.

papers.title: Headache in juvenile idiopathic arthritis: more common and phenotypically different than expected.
papers.abstract: Headache is among the most common neurological complaints in childhood and can substantially impair quality of life. Although children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) experience chronic inflammation and recurrent pain, the prevalence and phenotype of primary headache in this population remain insufficiently studied. This cross-sectional case-control study was conducted in a tertiary pediatric rheumatology clinic between October and December 2025. A total of 109 children with JIA and 125 age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HCs) were included. Headache was assessed by structured questionnaire and neurological examination, and all diagnoses were established by a pediatric neurologist according to the International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition. Multivariable logistic regression was adjusted for age, sex, family history of migraine, perceived sleep insufficiency and body mass index. Primary headache was more frequent in children with JIA than in HCs (37.6% vs. 17.6%, p < 0.001). The excess was confined to tension-type headache (TTH; 22.9% vs. 4.8%, p < 0.001), whereas migraine was equally frequent (14.7% vs. 12.8%, p = 0.71). After adjustment, JIA remained associated with TTH (odds ratio [OR] 6.94, 95% confidence interval [CI] 2.62-18.39) but not with migraine (OR 1.81, 95% CI 0.79-4.13). Conversely, family history of migraine (OR 2.35, 95% CI 1.06-5.19) and perceived sleep insufficiency (OR 3.99, 95% CI 1.76-9.02) were associated with migraine but not TTH. No disease-related or treatment-related variable was associated with headache. Children with JIA show a selective excess of TTH rather than a uniform increase in primary headache, while established risk factors track with migraine. Systematic headache enquiry may improve recognition of this underrecognized comorbidity.

papers.title: Multidimensional relationship between physical health and the brain, mental health, and cognitive development in the ABCD cohort: A 10-year review and future directions.
papers.abstract: The Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study® provides an unprecedented opportunity to examine how physical health, mental health, and neurobiological and neurocognitive developmental trajectories intersect throughout adolescence. Findings to date highlight complex interactions between lifestyle behaviors (e.g., physical activity, screen use, diet, sleep) and cardiometabolic outcomes in relation to neurocognitive development. For example, physical activity and sports participation are linked to enhanced executive functioning and healthier brain morphology, whereas variation in cortical and subcortical structures are associated with obesity and sleep disturbances. Excessive screen use and inadequate sleep further correlate with adverse cardiometabolic profiles and poorer neurocognitive outcomes. These relationships are affected by sociodemographic factors, family and social context, and adverse childhood experiences, which may moderate health behaviors and their relationship to cardiometabolic health and neurocognitive development. For example, dietary patterns vary by sex, socioeconomic status, and race/ethnicity, and signs of poor cardiometabolic health (hypertension, dyslipidemia, and obesity) emerge early, showing disparities across demographic groups. Subsequent alterations in neurobiological pathways may then contribute to the persistence of chronic disease risk in these populations. Additionally, pubertal onset, genetics, and medication use may play a role in neurobiological and neurocognitive trajectories and should be considered when conducting analyses. Together, these findings underscore the bidirectional and potentially cyclical nature of the interaction between physical health, mental health, and neurocognitive development, which are shaped by genetic, biological, and social-environmental factors. Future research leveraging ABCD's longitudinal design will be essential for disentangling causal pathways and informing interventions that promote health equity and optimize adolescent health.

papers.title: PRISM-MP: Psychology-guided and reliability-aware multimodal learning for cross-musician emotion recognition during musical performance.
papers.abstract: Emotion classification during active musical performance is challenging because neural activity, cardiac dynamics, and acoustic expression provide complementary but non-equivalent evidence of intended emotional communication and self-reported affect. This study presents PRISM-MP, a psychology-guided and reliability-aware multimodal framework for cross-musician emotion recognition. We analyzed a publicly available dataset comprising synchronized electroencephalography, electrocardiography, and musical audio recordings from 11 experienced musicians who performed excerpts intended to communicate happiness, sadness, anger, or relaxation. PRISM-MP integrates dynamic frequency-specific electroencephalographic functional graphs with affine-invariant tangent-space covariance representations, models multiscale physiological dynamics, and applies class-conditional source-domain alignment to reduce musician-specific distributional differences. The physiological and acoustic pathways receive auxiliary supervision from felt and communicated valence-arousal ratings, respectively. Their contributions are dynamically adjusted according to signal quality, predictive uncertainty, and cross-modal disagreement. Under nested source-only leave-one-musician-out evaluation, PRISM-MP achieved a musician-macro-averaged performance-level accuracy of 92.14%, balanced accuracy of 91.82%, macro-F1 of 0.910, Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.892, and expected calibration error of 0.041. Against the strongest recent source-only EEG baseline evaluated under the same protocol, the corresponding gains were 3.91 percentage points in balanced accuracy and 0.037 in macro-F1. The framework remained robust when electrocardiography or audio was unavailable and under partial electroencephalographic channel loss. A systematic leave-one-channel-out analysis across 29 EEG electrodes revealed nonuniform channel sensitivity. Removing C3, Cz, C4, and F3 produced the largest balanced-accuracy reductions of 2.22, 2.05, 2.02, and 1.90 percentage points, respectively, while removal of several other channels produced minimal changes. Computational profiling indicated 3.46 million trainable parameters and processing times of 74 ms with GPU-supported audio embedding and 312 ms on a desktop CPU, while physiological encoding and fusion required 18.7 ms after feature preparation. These timings exclude the 30-s observation period and do not represent end-to-end interactive latency. A secondary post hoc within-recording calibration analysis increased macro-F1 to 0.946 using a lightweight residual adapter. These findings support reliability-aware physiological-acoustic modeling as a computational foundation for future musician-centered affective interfaces.

papers.title: Time-dependent alterations of the heart-brain axis in rats following a single microwave exposure.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the time-dependent changes and possible mechanisms of the heart-brain axis in rats following S-band microwave exposure. A single microwave exposure model was established using 8-week-old male Wistar rats (2.856 GHz, 50 mW/cm², 30 min). At Days 1, 3, and 7 post-exposure, we evaluated electrocardiogram, heart rate variability, and electroencephalogram activities, alongside serum biochemical and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay indicators. Integrated transcriptomic and proteomic analyses of the hippocampus and myocardium, combined with real-time quantitative PCR, were utilized to validate key molecular changes. The results showed that following a single exposure, the function of the rat heart-brain axis changed in a time-dependent but outcome-specific manner: neuroendocrine, autonomic, and electroencephalographic alterations were most evident on Day 1, most circulating cardiac and brain injury markers were highest on Day 3, and lactate dehydrogenase increased only on Day 7. These changes were primarily characterized by imbalanced autonomic nervous function and heart rate variability, abnormal electrocardiogram and electroencephalogram activities, and elevated injury-related markers. Integrated multi-omics analysis revealed significant molecular remodeling in both tissues on Day 3. Myocardial differential molecules were primarily enriched in cytochrome P450-mediated metabolism and detoxification pathways, with representative molecules including Adh6 and Cyp4f5. Hippocampal differential molecules mainly involved neuroactive ligand-receptor interactions, neural signal transduction, and synaptic regulation pathways, with representative molecules including Adra2b and Chrna3. These findings suggest that a S-band microwave exposure induces heart-brain axis autonomic regulatory imbalance, electrophysiological abnormalities, and synchronized changes in central neural signaling and peripheral metabolic detoxification. These results provide an experimental basis for risk assessment and protective strategies against high-power microwaves.

papers.title: Machine learning classification of depression across three population cohorts using clinical, lifestyle, and multi-omics data.
papers.abstract: Depression is one of the leading global health issues, affecting over 280 million people. The etiology of depression is complex and multifactorial. The amalgamation of these diverse factors may yield valuable predictive insights, which are instrumental in formulating strategies for the prevention, early diagnosis, and timely intervention of depression. This study developed and validated machine learning-based models for depression risk prediction and classification using data from three cohorts: the UK Biobank (UKB), the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), and the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS). The integrated features included clinical data, lifestyle factors, and omics data (proteomics and metabolomics). Model performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), sensitivity, and specificity. SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations) was used for model interpretation. The models demonstrated solid discrimination performance across all three cohorts (AUC: 0.73-0.79), and cross-cohort validation yielded test AUCs of 0.68 and 0.71. SHAP-based feature importance analysis revealed that economic factors, marital status, physical activity, and sleep duration were core predictors across populations, while risk factors such as education level and drinking status showed significant national differences. Although the multi-omics model did not significantly improve discrimination performance, it provided new insights into the biological mechanisms of depression. This study developed an interpretable machine learning framework for large-scale depression screening, offering valuable insights for the development of personalized public health interventions and clinical strategies. It holds promise for improving treatment outcomes for depression patients through earlier referral for diagnostic confirmation and population-level screening.

papers.title: Bed-sharing and actigraphic rest-activity rhythms in six-month-old infants: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: To examine whether habitual bed-sharing is associated with non-parametric rest-activity rhythm measures in six-month-old infants. Cross-sectional analysis of 194 infants (mean age 6.4 months, range 6.0 to 8.4) from the CPAPI birth cohort, Ribeirão Preto, Brazil. Infants wore an ankle actigraph for a median of 7.4 valid days (2.8 to 12.2). Relative amplitude (RA), interdaily stability (IS), intradaily variability (IV), L5 and M10 were derived from non-binarized activity counts. Infants reported to share a bed frequently or always (n = 99) were compared with those sharing never or occasionally (n = 95) using Mann-Whitney tests and linear regression adjusted for infant sex and socioeconomic status, with false discovery rate correction. Bed-sharing was not associated with any rest-activity rhythm measure. Adjusted differences were small, with 95% confidence intervals excluding effects above 0.44 standard deviations in either direction (RA 0.009, 95% CI -0.014 to 0.032; IS -0.007, -0.038 to 0.024; IV 0.003, -0.044 to 0.050; L5 -27.5 counts/min, -76.2 to 21.2; M10 -57.1 counts/min, -343.4 to 229.2). Conclusions were unchanged after adjustment for maternal age, breastfeeding, light exposure, maternal employment, infant sleep difficulties and age, and in analyses restricted to comparable recording lengths, singletons and term infants. In an exploratory contrast, infants with inconsistent bed-sharing (occasionally or frequently, n = 40) had higher M10 than infants with consistent arrangements (never or always). Habitual bed-sharing was not associated with actigraphic rest-activity rhythm measures at six months. The estimates exclude moderate or large differences but not small ones, and do not support inferences about circadian mechanisms.

papers.title: Hypoxic burden versus apnea-hypopnea index as a predictor of cardiovascular outcomes in obstructive sleep apnea: A systematic review.
papers.abstract: The apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) remains the metric for grading obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) severity, although its association with cardiovascular (CV) outcomes is inconsistent. Hypoxic burden (HB) integrates the depth and duration of respiratory event-related oxygen desaturations and may better reflect OSA-related physiological stress. We evaluated the association between HB and CV outcomes and its prognostic information relative to AHI. We conducted a systematic review according to PRISMA 2020 recommendations and the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) guideline. PubMed, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to August 2026. The primary synthesis included independent cohort-level estimates reporting adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) per 1-standard deviation (SD) increase in HB, which were presented in a forest plot without a pooled estimate and synthesized by direction of effect. Within-study HB and AHI associations were compared descriptively. Eleven publications reporting 14 analyses from seven cohorts or trials were included. Four independent cohort-level estimates were available for the primary synthesis. All four indicated higher CV risk with increasing HB (HRs per 1-SD increase 1.13-1.45); the 95% CI excluded the null in three estimates and reached it in the fourth. Given the small number of estimates, these were not pooled. In a descriptive synthesis of eight within-study comparisons, HB showed a significant positive association with CV outcomes, whereas AHI showed no consistent positive association and was inversely associated with CV mortality in one MrOS analysis. In a single post hoc analysis of RICCADSA, high HB was associated with increased MACCE risk even among participants with relatively low AHI. Across individual community-based cohorts and populations with established cardiovascular disease and OSA, higher HB was consistently associated with increased CV morbidity and mortality, with modest effect sizes, and may provide prognostic information not fully captured by AHI. Given the small number of independent cohorts and the descriptive nature of the synthesis, these findings should be regarded as hypothesis-generating. These findings support a pathophysiologically informed, multidimensional assessment of OSA severity and CV risk. Prospective studies should standardize HB measurement, establish actionable thresholds, validate incremental prognostic value, and determine whether HB-guided risk stratification improves clinical outcomes.

papers.title: Performance evaluation of smart ring-derived sleep parameters compared with portable electroencephalography in university students.
papers.abstract: Wearable devices enable convenient assessment of sleep in daily life. Smart rings facilitate long-term monitoring; however, their agreement with electroencephalography (EEG)-based sleep assessment remains unclear. We evaluated the performance of the SOXAI RING -derived sleep parameters against those obtained using a portable EEG device. Of 52 university students enrolled, 49 (mean age 19.3 years; 42 females) were included in the final analysis. Participants underwent simultaneous overnight monitoring with the SOXAI RING (SOXAI Co., Ltd.) and portable EEG device (Proassist Co., Ltd.) under habitual home sleeping conditions. Total sleep time (TST), sleep onset latency (SOL), wake after sleep onset (WASO), and sleep stages were compared between devices. Epoch-by-epoch (EBE) analyses were also performed to evaluate sleep-wake and four-stage sleep classification. A strong correlation for TST was observed between devices (ρ = 0.70, p < 0.01). Bland-Altman analysis showed that the SOXAI RING tended to underestimate TST and light sleep, while overestimating WASO and deep sleep. In EBE analysis, the SOXAI RING showed high sensitivity for sleep but low specificity for wake. For four-stage classification, the overall accuracy was 50.0% and Cohen's κ was 0.27. The SOXAI RING showed good performance for estimating TST and may be useful for long-term sleep monitoring under habitual home conditions. However, EBE analysis demonstrated limited performance for wake detection and sleep-stage classification. Sleep-stage estimates and sleep fragmentation metrics should therefore be interpreted cautiously, and further refinement of sleep-staging algorithms is warranted.

papers.title: Does recovery sleep structure influence cognitive performance in healthy sleep deprived individuals? A scoping review.
papers.abstract: Given the critical role of recovery after sleep loss in many professional settings, this scoping review analysed studies linking the structure of recovery sleep to cognitive restoration in sleep-deprived healthy adults. In accordance with PRISMA guidelines, four electronic databases were searched using keywords covering three concepts: acute sleep deprivation/restriction, neurocognitive performance, and recovery sleep. Eligible studies measured sleep parameters during recovery, from a brief nap to several nights, following total sleep deprivation or sleep restriction, using objective monitoring (actigraphy or polysomnography), and assessed cognition objectively. Paediatric, adolescent and elderly populations were excluded. A total of 31 studies were included, with considerable heterogeneity in design. The main sleep parameters were total sleep time and markers of homeostatic regulation (slow-wave sleep duration and slow-wave activity), and the main cognitive domains were sustained attention and memory. Total sleep time emerged as the most important factor for cognitive recovery after sleep deprivation/restriction, though recovery also depended on recent sleep history. Slow-wave activity and sleep microstructure may explain interindividual differences in restoration. Most associations, however, rely on group-level comparisons rather than interindividual correlations, and the cognitive functions studied remain limited. Further studies should assess correlations between sleep parameters and cognitive recovery and improve reproducibility.

papers.title: The Effects of Nonpharmacologic Interventions to Enhance Sleep Outcomes Among Older People With Mild Cognitive Impairment: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effects of nonpharmacologic interventions on sleep outcomes in older adults with mild cognitive impairment (MCI). A systematic review and meta-analysis. Older people with MCI. A comprehensive search of MEDLINE, CINAHL, EMBASE, and PsycINFO was conducted from inception through June 2025 to identify eligible randomized controlled trials. Meta-analyses were conducted using RevMan when appropriate; narrative synthesis was used when pooling was not feasible. Sensitivity analyses explored the influence of study quality on outcomes. Fourteen randomized controlled trials, involving 874 participants, met the inclusion criteria. Exercise and cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) were the most frequently studied interventions, each examined in 4 trials. Two studies implemented multicomponent interventions integrating behavioral, cognitive, and lifestyle strategies. Other alternative interventions included transcranial magnetic stimulation, hypnosis, breath-based relaxation, and sport stacking. Pooled analysis showed that exercise significantly improved subjective sleep quality compared with controls (standardized mean difference, -1.78; 95% CI, -3.38 to -0.17; P = .03; I2 = 97%). CBT-I demonstrated a smaller but statistically significant effect (standardized mean difference, -0.85; 95% CI, -1.66 to -0.04; P = .04; I2 = 80%). Sensitivity analyses excluding a high-risk study without blinded assessors yielded reduced but still significant effects. Only a few studies included objective sleep measures, limiting conclusions about physiological outcomes. Multicomponent interventions showed potential benefits, but substantial variability in design indicates the need for standardized development frameworks. Alternative approaches, including transcranial magnetic stimulation, hypnosis, and relaxation therapy, showed preliminary promise but require further rigorous validation. Nonpharmacologic interventions, particularly exercise and CBT-I, demonstrate potential in improving subjective sleep quality among older adults with MCI. Rigorous research is needed to validate these findings on objective sleep outcomes and to establish robust frameworks for developing and optimizing multicomponent interventions that integrate behavioral and physiological mechanisms to support sleep and cognitive health in this at-risk population.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Medical Directors Association

papers.title: Implementation of nurse-led frontal electroencephalography for early neurological assessment in patients after cardiac arrest: the FRONT study.
papers.abstract: Continuous electroencephalography (cEEG) is a valuable tool for neurological prognostication after cardiac arrest. However, registration is often delayed by time-consuming electrode placement and limited availability of EEG technicians. This study investigated the implementation of a frontal EEG (fEEG) configuration using 6 self-adhesive electrodes by nurses within 3 h of Intensive Care Unit (ICU) admission in patients after cardiac arrest. The FRONT study followed a type 3 hybrid design. Nurses were trained to start an fEEG through a theoretical and practical session and were supported by a Step-by-Step interactive guide. Knowledge, attitude, and practice surveys were completed by nurses at baseline and after each fEEG application. Correct and timely application was measured prospectively in 60 patients. At baseline, the survey response rate was 46% (49/107); after application, it was 68% (41/60). Most nurses (84%) reported having sufficient knowledge of fEEG electrode placement and monitoring. The interactive guide was frequently used (98%) during fEEG initiation; the median application time was 20 min [IQR: 15-25]. All nurses found early fEEG monitoring meaningful; perception improved since implementation (3.98 ± 0.78 vs 4.54 ± 0.51, p < 0.001). During the implementation, an fEEG was applied in 88% of patients (53/60), including 73% (44/60) within 3 h. Electrode placement was confirmed as correct by EEG technicians in all evaluated patients. ICU nurses were able to apply fEEG monitoring with high levels of adoption, acceptability and fidelity following a short, multifaceted training program combined with an interactive guide. Further research is needed to clarify the interpretability, diagnostic performance, prognostic value, and clinical utility of nurse-led fEEG monitoring in post-resuscitation care. Early bedside EEG assessment by trained ICU nurses may facilitate timely neurological evaluation in routine clinical practice.

papers.title: Individual deviation network analysis and rat multiomics profiling link sleep deprivation to depressive-like behavior and microbiome-metabolome remodeling.
papers.abstract: Disturbed sleep and depression are bidirectionally linked, but the peripheral biological pathway converting chronic sleep loss into a depressive phenotype remains poorly defined. We combined a human individual deviation network (IDN) analysis with a rat sleep deprivation model to investigate changes in colonic mucosal morphology and tight junction protein levels, microbiome-metabolome reorganization, and candidate fecal metabolite signatures. An IDN was constructed in 14,769 NHANES adults (2009-2018) using 14 variables spanning sleep, depression, diet-microbiome, glucolipid, and hepato-renal domains. Two-sample Mendelian randomization provided directional annotations. Male Sprague-Dawley rats underwent modified multiple platform sleep deprivation for 18 h/day over 21 days (n = 5/group). Behavioral, intestinal, inflammatory, microbial, and fecal metabolomic endpoints were assessed, and metabolite covariation modules were used to identify behavior-linked Hub metabolites. The IDN identified Sleep × Depression as the dominant deviation axis, with joint amplification extending to the diet-microbiome (dietary index) and metabolic domains. In rats, sleep deprivation reduced sucrose preference and increased forced swim immobility without altering total fluid intake or open field distance. Colonic ZO-1, Occludin, and Claudin-1 decreased while serum TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 increased. Fecal microbiome and metabolome were remodeled. Module M06 was the only FDR-supported behavior-linked module, localizing to docosapentaenoic acid (22:5n-6), FAHFA 38:5, and N-oleoylethanolamine as Hub metabolites. Sleep × Depression emerged as the dominant clinical axis capturing individual heterogeneity beyond group means. In a complementary rat model, chronic sleep deprivation produced depressive-like behavior, inflammation, and microbiome-metabolome remodeling, together with colonic mucosal alterations and reduced tight junction protein expression suggestive of impaired barrier integrity. The M06 hub metabolites are candidate fecal biomarkers and molecules for future mechanistic studies of sleep deprivation-related depression.

papers.title: A post-training quantization framework for EEG-based sleep stage classification.
papers.abstract: Sleep classification models play a crucial role in assessing sleep quality. Although the classification performance of these models has continuously improved in recent years, significant accuracy degradation is commonly observed when quantizing and deploying them on edge devices with limited memory and computational resources. To address this challenge, we propose a posttraining quantization framework for EEG-based sleep stage classification. Specifically, we first identify convolutional and linear layers within the model, then compute layerwise sensitivities based on each layer's input. We dynamically adjust the threshold for each layer based on its sensitivity, using this threshold to detect abnormal weights causing excessive quantization error in that layer. To ensure quantization accuracy, we preserve these abnormal weights at their original precision while compressing the remaining weights to 4 bits. After quantizing each layer, we employ dynamic low-rank compensation to correct quantization errors and further enhance accuracy, addressing information loss during quantization. Experiments on the Sleep-EDF-20, Sleep-EDF-78 and SHHS datasets demonstrate that our method achieves near-lossless compression: the accuracy of the vast majority of sleep classification models drops by less than 1%, while reducing model size by nearly 8 times. This work provides the first general framework for post-training quantization of sleep classification models, offering a new approach for the practical deployment of these models on edge devices.

papers.title: Bayesian Complete-Pooling in Cross-Subject Classification for Motor Imagery Electroencephalogram.
papers.abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have long sought calibration-free operation, yet classifiers are typically benchmarked on discrimination alone. Discrimination is blind to calibration, a meaningful gap given that electroencephalogram (EEG) signals are nonstationary and point-estimate classifiers can become overconfident under distribution shift. We conducted a large-scale study contrasting Bayesian complete-pooling models against frequentist baselines for cross-subject, left-hand versus right-hand motor imagery EEG classification across 20 datasets. Each of six frequentist pipelines was paired with an analogous Bayesian pipeline sharing identical, deterministic feature extraction, so that only the classifier was Bayesian. Bayesian classifiers were fit via Markov chain Monte Carlo posterior sampling. Our primary metric was the Brier score, decomposed into reliability and resolution, alongside the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve for discrimination and Shannon entropy for sharpness. For each metric we fit a random-effects meta-analysis with Knapp-Hartung adjustment, verified by leave-one-out influence analysis. Bayesian complete-pooling produced statistically significant improvements in reliability and increases in predictive uncertainty (lower sharpness), with 95% confidence intervals of [-0.0029, -0.0001] for reliability and [0.0022, 0.0220] bits for entropy. Still, neither effect held statistical significance when datasets with flagged posterior sampling were excluded. Brier score, resolution, and discrimination showed no significant differences. Between-study heterogeneity was low across all metrics. Bayesian pipelines consumed roughly thirteen times more energy than their frequentist counterparts, a cost that remains modest relative to common household appliances. This modest cost makes partial-pooling across subjects and sessions, the structure complete-pooling omits, a feasible next step.

papers.title: BCI-FIT: Feasibility of a customization protocol for communication brain-computer interface systems.
papers.abstract: The BCI Functional Implementation Toolkit (BCI-FIT) is a flexible, user-centered, interdisciplinary customization protocol for non-implantable communication brain-computer interface (cBCI) systems. Here we describe the protocol and present results of a non-experimental exploratory study of the feasibility of this approach and its effects on accuracy, speed, and user experience. Five participants with speech and/or physical impairments resulting from amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) completed calibration and copy-spelling tasks with both customized and non-customized versions of a non-implantable cBCI over multiple visits. System customization was adjusted after each visit based on typing performance, participant preferences, clinical observations, brain signal characteristics, and results of simulations and other offline exploration. Three participants demonstrated consistently high typing accuracy under both conditions, with better typing speed and/or user experience under the customized condition. Two participants had low typing accuracy that did not improve with system customization. The subset of parameters modified, and how they were modified, varied widely across participants due to their different needs and preferences. Participants with high typing accuracy reported that system customization led to improvements in comfort, workload, typing performance, and aesthetic appeal. Customization may improve cBCI typing performance and user experience for some individuals with disabilities, but additional investigation is needed. Participant preferences, clinical observations, brain-signal characteristics, simulation results, and typing performance all influenced customization decisions. Additional customization options could support successful cBCI use for a wider range of users.

papers.title: Capacity-controlled EEG denoising: diminishing reconstruction returns on semi-synthetic benchmarks and task-dependent downstream utility.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) denoising is often ranked by clean-reference reconstruction metrics, although downstream task performance is less often assessed. We tested capacity effects and when reconstruction fidelity tracks utility.Approach. A depthwise-separable convolutional denoiser spanned 1.05K-40.26K parameters. Capacity was evaluated on semi-synthetic clean-reference benchmarks (EEGDenoiseNet and a mixed-artifact corpus) and by zero-shot reconstruction on brain-computer interface (BCI) Competition IV-2a/IV-2b. Downstream effects and same-condition metric-utility associations used IV-2a motor imagery, with subjects as inferential units (n=9). Further tests used an IV-2b cross-session replication and within-subject paired-recording sleep staging in 75 Sleep-EDF subjects.Main results. In these semi-synthetic reconstruction settings, capacity effects depended on metric and dataset. Electrooculographic (EOG) reconstruction improved from base8 to base16 (correlation-coefficient increment 0.007264, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.005525-0.009002), whereas electromyographic (EMG) correlation coefficient met the selected practical-saturation criterion from base6 to base8. These intervals are conditional on fixed benchmark source pools; a source-level bootstrap left both classifications unchanged. On IV-2a, matched denoising reduced common spatial patterns with linear discriminant analysis (CSP+LDA) accuracy for EOG (Δ=-0.057, 95% CI -0.087 to -0.029), EMG (-0.102, -0.152 to -0.056), and mixed contamination (-0.099, -0.152 to -0.046); these effects were supported under Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate (BH-FDR) control, not Holm familywise control. ShallowFBCSPNet and EEGConformer showed reductions in several conditions, whereas EEGNet and Deep4Net had no multiplicity-corrected effects. Reconstruction metrics were associated with downstream change in some EMG/mixed conditions but not consistently for EOG. In Sleep-EDF paired-recording validation, denoisers reduced sleep-stage balanced accuracy under synthetic-EOG and unmodified-recording controls; base16 changes were -0.050 and -0.074. IV-2b effects were near-null under the evaluated 01T/02T-to-03T cross-session protocol.Significance. Reconstruction fidelity is informative but not a universal surrogate endpoint. Capacity claims from semi-synthetic benchmarks should distinguish formal practical saturation from diminishing returns, and denoising evaluation should report subject-level effects and transfer controls.

papers.title: Interventions to Support Healthy Movement Behaviors Among Preschool Children in Early Childhood Education and Care Settings: Protocol for a Realist Synthesis.
papers.abstract: A paradigm shift toward a broader view of movement behaviors emphasizes the importance of physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep across the 24-hour day. Despite these behaviors being positively associated with important health and development outcomes, research suggests that many preschool children worldwide fail to meet the World Health Organization 24-hour movement behavior guidelines. To improve adherence, interventions have often targeted early childhood education and care settings, key environments where children spend a substantial proportion of their day. However, evidence regarding the effectiveness of these interventions and their components is inconsistent. These inconsistencies highlight the complexity of movement behavior interventions, as movement behaviors are interdependent and influenced by multiple contextual factors. Considering this, a theory-driven approach is best suited to develop a deeper understanding of what works for whom, under which circumstances, and how, ultimately improving policy and intervention development. The aim of this protocol is to investigate under which contextual circumstances interventions most effectively improve preschool children's 24-hour movement behaviors in early childhood education and care settings by developing an evidence-informed initial program theory that outlines for whom these interventions work, under what contexts, and through which mechanisms. Findings from the synthesis will be reported in accordance with the RAMESES (Realist and Meta-Narrative Evidence Synthesis: Evolving Standards) publication standards. A literature search will be conducted to identify relevant peer-reviewed movement behavior intervention studies. Identified studies will be considered for inclusion based on predetermined inclusion criteria. Study screening, data extraction, and quality assessment will be independently conducted by 2 reviewers. The realist synthesis will apply a combined conceptual framework to develop potential context-mechanism-outcome configurations and an initial program theory, which will be refined-through piecemeal confirmation and/or disconfirmation-during the evidence synthesis. Duplicate screening, quality assessment, data extraction, relevance and rigor appraisal, and iterative program theory testing are planned for completion by the end of 2026. The primary review manuscript is targeted for submission by early 2027. This review shifts away from the current literature's focus on intervention effectiveness and instead develops a more nuanced understanding of intervention implementation and effectiveness by applying theory-driven processes. The results of the synthesis intend to identify appropriate strategies to promote healthy 24-hour movement behaviors in the early years to inform the development, adaptation, and implementation of current and future interventions. papers.title: Risk Factors for Normal-tension Glaucoma Progression: A Review.
papers.abstract: This review identified disc hemorrhages, intraocular pressure variability, and systemic vascular dysregulation as consistent predictors of normal-tension glaucoma progression, highlighting the need for risk stratification to guide individualized treatment, follow-up, and prognosis. Normal-tension glaucoma (NTG) is characterized by progressive optic neuropathy despite intraocular pressure (IOP) consistently within the conventionally defined normal limits. While some patients remain stable without treatment, others progress rapidly to irreversible vision loss. This review summarizes current evidence on predictive factors for NTG progression to support future risk stratification tools that aid clinical decision-making and prognosis. A comprehensive search of PubMed, CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO ICTRP identified studies published between 2015 and 2025. Eligible studies included meta-analyses, clinical trials, cohort studies, case-control studies, and case series evaluating predictive factors for NTG onset or progression. Forty-five studies met inclusion criteria. Reported predictors include clinical biomarkers (female sex, younger age, labile IOP), imaging structural biomarkers (retinal nerve fibre layer thinning, macular ganglion cell-inner plexiform layer loss), corneal biomechanics (low corneal hysteresis, high deformability), optic disc morphology (tilted discs, lamina cribrosa defects, disc haemorrhages), systemic/vascular factors (nocturnal hypotension, ocular perfusion pressure variability, migraine, Raynaud's phenomenon, obstructive sleep apnoea), and genetic predispositions. NTG progression results from IOP-dependent and IOP-independent mechanisms. Among predictors, disc haemorrhages, IOP variability, and systemic vascular dysregulation emerge as the most consistent indicators of progression. Identifying at-risk patients is essential for tailoring treatment and follow-up, preventing overtreatment in stable cases, and avoiding irreversible sight loss. Future research could establish practical prognostic tools based on the most influential risk factors.

papers.title: 'Therapeutic potential of resveratrol against REM sleep deprivation-induced memory deficits: involvement of hippocampal BDNF and TrkB protein expression.
papers.abstract: Sleep plays a crucial role in the formation and consolidation of memory, as well as in the regulation of memory-related protein expression. Sleep deprivation (SD) has detrimental effects on cognitive function. Resveratrol is a natural polyphenol with reported neuroprotective properties. This study investigated the effects of resveratrol on REM sleep deprivation-induced memory impairment and hippocampal BDNF and TrkB protein expression. Fear conditioning assessed memory, while the multiple-platform apparatus induced rapid eye movement sleep deprivation (REM-SD). Beginning 24 h after training, rats underwent 6 h of REM-SD daily for four consecutive days. Resveratrol (10 or 40 mg/kg) was administered intraperitoneally immediately before or after REM-SD, according to treatment condition. Hippocampal tissue was collected for Western blot analysis of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB) protein expression. REM-SD impaired fear-memory performance, as reflected by reduced freezing and increased latency to freezing. Pre-treatment with 40 mg/kg resveratrol attenuated these REM-SD-induced behavioral impairments, whereas post-treatment with both 10 and 40 mg/kg showed protective effects. REM-SD also reduced hippocampal BDNF and TrkB protein expression, and treatment with 40 mg/kg resveratrol attenuated these reductions, restoring protein expression toward control levels. This study provided evidence that resveratrol attenuates REM-SD-induced fear memory impairment, and this effect is associated with the preservation of hippocampal BDNF and TrkB protein expression.

papers.title: Wearable automated cough detection in horses with chronic cough: model development, validation, and exploratory associations in asthma.
papers.abstract: Coughing is a nonspecific respiratory sign that is common in horses with asthma. Cough quantification is currently subjective and labor-intensive, leaving its diagnostic and monitoring potential underexplored. (1) Develop a wearable audio recorder for horses; (2) collect recordings of coughing horses and annotate coughs; (3) train a machine learning model to automate cough detection; and (4) describe temporal patterns of coughing and determine pathophysiologic correlations in horses with asthma. Seventy horses were recruited from a teaching herd, clinical cases, and via social media. Sixty had coughing for ≥3 weeks and valid recordings. In our prospective observational and analytical study, coughs were recorded using a digital device, annotated by a single observer, and used to develop a machine-learning-based cough-detection pipeline. Machine learning output was analyzed using generalized linear mixed models to determine circadian patterns and pathophysiologic associations of coughing. We annotated 252 of 1260 recorded hours. We labeled 8555 sound events, 2780 of which were coughs of the instrumented horse. Our machine learning model detected coughs with a sensitivity of 0.95 and a specificity of 0.9993. In horses with asthma, coughing frequency was associated with neutrophilic lung inflammation and showed a diurnal pattern with peak rates around 3 am. The combination of robust hardware for long-term recordings and high-performance machine learning algorithms has the potential to transform coughing from a relatively crude clinical sign to a quantifiable endpoint in research and clinical practice.

papers.title: Environmental enrichment enhances hepatic oxidative stress and antioxidant defenses without modulating immunometabolic gene expression in adult male mice.
papers.abstract: Environmental enrichment (EE) is a non-pharmacological intervention based on modifications of the housing environment that increase sensory, cognitive, and motor stimulation, and it has been proposed to modulate immunometabolic responses. To investigate the effects of EE on hepatic redox status, oxidative balance, and immunometabolic gene expression in healthy mice. Male C57BL/6 mice were randomly assigned at 45 days of age to a standard environment (SE; n = 7) or an enriched environment (EE; n = 7) for six weeks. The EE group was housed in larger cages containing (tunnels, nesting material, and objects changed weekly). After euthanasia, liver samples were analyzed by spectrophotometric assays for NAD ⁺ /NADH, lipid peroxidation (TBARS), protein carbonylation, antioxidant enzyme activities (SOD, CAT, GST), GSH/GSSG ratio, and total sulfhydryl groups. Hepatic expression of inflammatory, metabolic, and mitochondrial genes was assessed by RT-qPCR (n = 4 per group). EE was associated with lower hepatic NAD⁺ (p = 0.001) and higher NADH (p = 0.006), lower lipid peroxidation (p = 0.004) and protein carbonylation (p = 0.009), and higher antioxidant enzyme activities. The GSH/GSSG ratio (p = 0.04) and sulfhydryl content (p = 0.001) were also higher. No significant changes were observed in the expression of the genes analyzed. Six weeks of EE were associated with changes in hepatic redox status, with lower oxidative damage markers and higher antioxidant defenses, without detectable changes in the expression of the genes analyzed. These findings suggest that short-term EE optimizes hepatic redox balance and antioxidant defenses, while noting that future studies with extended exposure and pathological models will clarify its long-term transcriptional and structural impacts.

papers.title: Automated action potential parameter analysis for reproducible electrophysiological measurements in neurons.
papers.abstract: Quantitative analysis of action potential (AP) waveforms is central to studies of neuronal excitability, ion channel function, disease mechanisms and pharmacological modulation. However, AP analysis is still often performed using partially manual workflows or proprietary software environments that can constrain the amount of information extracted from APs and limit reproducibility, transparency and throughput. Here, we present a freely available, open-source software tool for extracting AP parameters, developed for use with the OriginLab software package Origin/OriginPro. APpar detects APs from membrane voltage recordings using a user-defined derivative criterion and calculates a comprehensive set of excitability parameters, including resting membrane potential, voltage threshold, overshoot, afterhyperpolarization (AHP), AP amplitude, rise and decay time, AP duration, AP half-width, AP width at 0 mV, AP area above voltage threshold, dV/dtmax, dV/dtmin and interspike interval for the respective AP. Because AP threshold is a particularly sensitive and method-dependent measurement, APpar includes a TRUE-threshold validation algorithm. After the initial forward dV/dt threshold crossing is identified, the software finds AP overshoot, searches backward to the closest preceding local dV/dt maximum, then searches backward to the user-defined dV/dt crossing and recalculates AP parameters from this validated threshold point. We validated APpar using APs from dorsal root ganglion neuron current-clamp recordings, including copied identical APs, current-evoked repetitive firing and long-duration spontaneous firing. The software produced stable measurements from identical copied APs and extracted dynamic changes in AP parameters across repetitive and spontaneous firing sequences. APpar provides a transparent, customizable and Origin-compatible framework for reproducible AP analysis in neuronal electrophysiology. KEY POINTS: Action potential (AP) waveforms contain important information about neuronal excitability and function of the underlying ion channels, but their analysis is often performed using partially manual, labour-intensive workflows, constraining the amount of information extracted from each AP, which can limit reproducibility and throughput. Measurements such as AP threshold, amplitude and duration depend strongly on how threshold is defined, creating variability between studies and laboratories. We developed APpar, a freely available open-source software tool that automatically detects APs and extracts a comprehensive set of waveform and excitability parameters within the widely used Origin/OriginPro environment. APpar incorporates a novel TRUE-threshold (Temporally Reversed Unsupervised Extraction of the Threshold) validation algorithm that improves the consistency of derivative-based threshold detection while preserving user control over physiologically meaningful analysis settings. Validation using dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neuron recordings showed that APpar provides stable measurements and enables efficient analysis of single AP, repetitive and spontaneous firing, supporting reproducible studies of neuronal excitability and ion channel function.

papers.title: A Neuro-Inspired Dual-Pathway Attention Network for EEG-Based Identity Recognition.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) signals have shown promise for biometric recognition due to their intrinsic liveness detection. However, their practical deployment remains limited. The main obstacles are non-stationary drift, scarce labeled data, and fluctuating signal quality. Most existing models adopt static computation graphs, which are ill-equipped to handle these variations. We propose a dual-pathway architecture that separates a data-driven bottom-up perceptual extractor from a prior-guided top-down modulator. A quality-aware gate computes instantaneous signal stability from channel-wise and temporal variances. It dynamically fuses the two pathways: bottom-up features dominate when the signal is clean, and identity priors take over when noise is high. Deep residual connections and pyramid fusion stabilize multi-scale learning. On the DEAP dataset, our method achieves 93.8% accuracy, which is 5.3 percentage points higher than the best baseline. On THU-EP, it reaches 97.2%. In cross-session tests on the noisy SEED-IV dataset, performance drops only 2.5% in Session 2 and 5.2% in Session 3. With only 1% of the training data on THU-EP, the model still attains 76.8% accuracy. Dynamic, signal-dependent fusion improves accuracy, cross-session robustness, and data efficiency. This work offers a practical, low-enrollment solution for patient identity verification, electronic health record access, and brain-computer interface authentication in clinical and mobile settings. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/cangtianhaoxue/ DPRAN.git.
papers.journal: IEEE journal of biomedical and health informatics

papers.title: Machine learning-assisted fusion of urinary Raman and fluorescence spectra for detection of urothelial carcinoma.
papers.abstract: Urothelial carcinoma (UC) diagnosis still relies on invasive procedures such as cystoscopy, motivating the development of non-invasive urine-based alternatives. Here, we investigate a multimodal spectroscopic approach combining Raman with UV-excited and VIS-excited fluorescence measurements for UC detection from unprocessed urine using fibre-optic probes. A cohort of 285 patients was analyzed, including 120 UC cases and 165 controls. Spectral analysis revealed consistent biochemical differences between groups, associated with variations in key urinary constituents such as NADH, flavins, porphyrins, urea, and amino acids, supporting the diagnostic potential of urine composition. Two machine learning strategies were evaluated. A PCA-LDA classifier integrating multimodal features achieved moderately low performance (∼64% accuracy), highlighting both the feasibility of spectral data fusion and the limitations of linear methods for complex datasets. In contrast, an artificial neural network (ANN) applied to full spectral data significantly improved classification performance, reaching accuracies above 90% when combined with data augmentation. These results demonstrate that the multimodal spectroscopy approach, particularly when coupled with advanced machine learning strategies, can enable effective non-invasive detection of UC. Despite limitations related to fibre-probe measurements and bulk urine variability, the proposed approach represents a promising step toward rapid and cost-effective bladder cancer screening.
papers.journal: Analytical methods : advancing methods and applications

papers.title: Associations Between Indoor Musty Odors and Sleep Quality and Duration Among Older Adults: Longitudinal Study.
papers.abstract: Indoor environmental air quality may influence sleep health among older adults. However, evidence on the association between indoor musty odors, a proxy for dampness- and mold-related exposures, and sleep outcomes remains limited. Susceptibility to environmental exposures may also vary by chronic lung disease status. This study aimed to examine the associations of indoor musty odors with sleep quality and sleep duration among older adults and to explore these associations across subgroups defined by chronic lung disease status. Data were drawn from 3 waves (2011-2018) of the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey. Community-dwelling older adults aged ≥65 years without cognitive impairment or dementia were included. Self-reported sleep quality was categorized as good, fair, or poor, and sleep duration was categorized as short (<7 hours), normal (7-8 hours), or long (>8 hours). Generalized estimating equation models with a logit link and an exchangeable working correlation structure were applied. Stabilized inverse probability of attrition weights was used to account for attrition. Models were adjusted for sociodemographic, health-related, lifestyle, and residential environmental factors. Analyses were conducted overall and stratified by chronic lung disease status. A total of 5712 participants were included, contributing 10,449 observations across 3 survey waves. At baseline, participants had a mean age of 82.4 (SD 10.0) years; 39.8% (n=2271) were aged ≥85 years, 52.7% (n=3010) were male, and 12.8% (n=732) had chronic lung disease. Overall, 17.6% (n=1008) reported indoor musty odors; 24.6% (n=1404) and 11.4% (n=650) reported fair and poor sleep quality, respectively; and 32% (n=1829) and 27.9% (n=1591) reported short and long sleep durations, respectively. Exposure to indoor musty odors was associated with higher odds of fair sleep quality (odds ratio [OR] 1.19, 95% CI 1.04-1.36; P=.01) and poor sleep quality (OR 1.63, 95% CI 1.37-1.95; P<.001), as well as short sleep duration (OR 1.36, 95% CI 1.19-1.55; P<.001). These associations were statistically significant among individuals without chronic lung disease (P=.02, P<.001, and P<.001, respectively) but not among those with chronic lung disease (P=.20, P=.12, and P=.10, respectively). Indoor musty odors were associated with adverse sleep outcomes among older adults, particularly among individuals without chronic lung disease. These findings highlight the importance of indoor air quality for sleep health and support interventions targeting dampness and mold in residential settings.

papers.title: Safety and efficacy of Streptococcus salivarius subsp. thermophilus ST36 in the improvement of gut and immune function: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the safety and efficacy of S. salivarius subsp. thermophilus ST36 in improving intestinal and immune functions. A total of 98 healthy adults were enrolled in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial and allocated to receive either ST36 (3 × 10¹⁰ CFU/day, n = 49) or placebo (n = 49) for 8 weeks. Participants were instructed to take the assigned preparation daily and record any adverse events. Gut microbiota composition, serum biomarkers, gastrointestinal function and quality of life were evaluated. A total of 85 participants completed the trial. This study was registered with the Clinical Trials Registry (No.: NCT06779994). ST36 supplementation was associated with a downward trend in serum calprotectin levels, approached statistical significance compared with placebo (p = 0.050), whereas LL-37 levels remained unchanged. Fecal microbiota analysis revealed significant enrichment of the butyrate-producing genus Anaerobutyricum and a concurrent reduction in Bacteroides in the ST36 group, accompanied by favorable, albeit non-significant, trends toward improved gastrointestinal symptom scores and stool type classification (assessed via the Bristol Stool Form Scale) relative to placebo. Sleep quality showed slight improvements in both groups without significant between-group differences. Throughout the 8-week intervention, ST36 exhibited a favorable safety profile, with stable hematological and biochemical parameters and no intervention-related adverse events or allergic reactions reported. ST36 supplementation was safe and well tolerated, induced targeted shifts in specific microbial taxa (notably enriching beneficial genera), and showed a favorable trend toward improving gastrointestinal outcomes, with indications of potential immune benefits.

papers.title: The association between Graves' disease, an autoimmune thyroid disorder, and early psychiatric background.
papers.abstract: Graves' disease is an autoimmune thyroid disorder; whether pre-existing psychiatric conditions precede its onset is unclear. Using Clalit Health Services records, we conducted a matched cohort study of 16,477 individuals with Graves' disease and 82,385 controls (1:5), matched on age, gender, and socioeconomic status. Psychiatric history (any recorded diagnosis or dispensed psychotropic medication) was assessed at least 10, 15, and 20 years before diagnosis by conditional logistic regression within matched sets, and by level of diagnostic certainty. A documented psychiatric history was significantly associated with subsequent Graves' disease at 10 years (OR = 1.16, 95% CI 1.10-1.22) and 15 years (OR = 1.13, 1.06-1.21). The association was confined to psychotropic dispensing without a recorded diagnosis (OR = 1.18, 1.11-1.25), mainly anxiolytics and hypnotics/sedatives; recorded diagnoses were not associated (OR = 1.01, 0.95-1.08), nor were mood disorders (80% power to detect an OR of 1.13). Schizophrenia was inversely associated (OR = 0.68, 0.56-0.82), persisting after adjustment for antipsychotics (OR = 0.69, 0.56-0.86). The association was significant in women but not men. The modest association reflects symptomatically treated anxiety and sleep complaints rather than diagnosed psychiatric illness; the inverse schizophrenia association may reflect shared HLA-region immunogenetics. Both findings require replication.
papers.journal: The world journal of biological psychiatry : the official journal of the World Federation of Societies of Biological Psychiatry

papers.title: A chronic pancreatitis pain program: comprehensive evaluation, treatment planning, and care for patients with chronic pancreatitis-related pain.
papers.abstract: Chronic pancreatitis (CP) is a multifactorial inflammatory syndrome frequently complicated by refractory abdominal pain. Current treatment strategies rely heavily on opioids and invasive surgical procedures. Structural pancreatic pathology correlates poorly with pain severity, and pancreas-independent mechanisms, including nociplastic and centrally mediated processes are increasingly recognized as contributors to pain but remain understood. We describe the Johns Hopkins Chronic Pancreatitis Pain Program, a multidisciplinary initiative integrating psychiatry, neurogastroenterology, pancreatology, and psychology. We present two patient-consented cases to illustrate the application of a neuromodulation-focused, multimodal treatment model. Both patients demonstrated clinically meaningful improvements in pain, mood, sleep, function, and quality of life following a comprehensive evaluation and targeted pharmacologic and behavioral interventions. In one case, opioid tapering accompanied symptomatic improvement. These cases illustrate the potential benefits of a multidisciplinary, neuromodulation-focused approach to CP-related pain. Longitudinal data collection is ongoing to further characterize treatment response and pain phenotypes.

papers.title: Integrating convolutional variational autoencoders and the Gaussian mixture model for efficient manifold learning and clustering of spatially preserved EEG topographic maps.
papers.abstract: EEG microstate analysis segments continuous brain activity into brief, quasi-stable topographic configurations whose quantity, duration, and transition dynamics index cognitive state and neuropsychiatric conditions. The standard algorithm, modified k-means (ModKMeans), operates in electrode space. It performs hard partitioning, assigning each data point to exactly one cluster, and provides no learned representation, no generative decoder, and no probabilistic soft assignment. In this research, a Convolutional Variational Deep Embedding model (Conv-VaDE) is designed, a topographic-map adaptation of Variational Deep Embedding (VaDE) that places a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) prior on the latent space of a convolutional variational autoencoder and jointly trains the encoder, decoder, and GMM. Microstate polarity invariance, the property that a topography [Formula: see text] and its sign-inverted counterpart [Formula: see text] index the same underlying configuration, is preserved through three coordinated mechanisms: sign-flip augmentation of the training set, a polarity-invariant reconstruction loss, and an encoder regulariser on the latent embedding. The model is evaluated on a sample of healthy participants ([Formula: see text] healthy adults, eyes-closed) from the LEMON resting-state EEG dataset using a multi-quadrant evaluation framework, with each method assessed in its native frame and cross-method comparisons performed via rank-based Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Conv-VaDE instead offers a focused set of capabilities the standard ModKMeans pipeline does not provide: a learned generative latent manifold (silhouette 0.232 at [Formula: see text], with very narrow cross-subject interquartile-range width [Formula: see text] across the 203 participants, indicating highly reproducible latent geometry), decoded GMM cluster centres inspectable as scalp topographies, probabilistic soft assignment for transitional states, and a generative framework supporting downstream representation analysis. A rank-based meta-criterion over silhouette, Calinski-Harabasz, and Davies-Bouldin yields modal [Formula: see text] for Conv-VaDE (39.4%) and [Formula: see text] for ModKMeans (29.6%); [Formula: see text] is adopted to align with the canonical Lehmann A/B/C/D literature. Within the classical cluster-validity register, ModKMeans attains a higher silhouette and 4-5 percentage points higher Global Explained Variance at every K (Wilcoxon, BH-corrected, [Formula: see text]). The two methods occupy distinct positions in the methodological design space, with the cross-method comparison characterising the trade-off between direct electrode-space optimisation and learned generative representation rather than adjudicating method superiority.

papers.title: Household-Level Effectiveness of Cypermethrin-Imidacloprid Combination Treatment for Cimex hemipterus Control: A Randomized Field Trial in Tehran, Iran.
papers.abstract: Bed bug (Cimex hemipterus) infestations are an increasing urban public health concern because they adversely affect skin health, sleep, psychological well-being, quality of life, and impose considerable economic costs on affected households. Despite the widespread use of pyrethroid insecticides, increasing resistance has reduced treatment effectiveness, and evidence from randomized household-based field trials evaluating alternative insecticide regimens remains limited. This study compared the effectiveness of cypermethrin monotherapy with a cypermethrin-imidacloprid combination for controlling household C. hemipterus infestations. We conducted a randomized household-level field study in Tehran, Iran, in which 600 households with confirmed C. hemipterus infestation were allocated equally to cypermethrin monotherapy or cypermethrin plus imidacloprid. Households were inspected on Days 1, 3, 7, 10, 14, and 30. The primary outcome was the absence of live bed bugs detected by visual inspection at Day 30. Sequencing of a subset of baseline specimens was performed to identify species and VGSC variants previously associated with pyrethroid resistance. All 600 households had a recorded Day-30 assessment. No live bed bugs were detected in 294/300 (98.0%) households receiving cypermethrin plus imidacloprid compared with 111/300 (37.0%) receiving cypermethrin alone (adjusted relative risk, 2.56; 95% CI 2.25-2.92; P < 0.001). Higher baseline infestation burden was associated with a lower probability of Day-30 absence of detectable live bed bugs. Molecular analysis of 75 reported specimens identified resistance-associated VGSC variants L1014F and M918I, without establishing phenotypic resistance. In this randomized household field study, the cypermethrin-imidacloprid regimen resulted in a substantially higher proportion of households with no visually detectable live bed bugs at Day 30 than cypermethrin monotherapy. However, the findings are limited to short-term entomological outcomes under the investigated field conditions. The study does not establish sustained eradication, insecticide synergy, phenotypic resistance, or a causal contribution of VGSC variants to treatment failure. Further studies incorporating longer follow-up, verified insecticide application records, and phenotypic susceptibility testing are warranted.

papers.title: Clinical correlates of sleep quality in idiopathic adult-onset dystonia.
papers.abstract: Idiopathic adult-onset dystonia (IAOD) is characterized by a broad spectrum of non-motor symptoms. Although sleep disorders can also be present in IAOD, data on sleep in dystonia are still limited. To understand demographic, motor, non-motor, and lifestyle factors associated with subjective sleep quality in IAOD. Patients with IAOD were recruited from consecutive outpatients attending the movement disorder clinics of five Italian movement disorder centres. In addition to demographic, lifestyle, and clinical information (on both motor and non-motor symptoms), the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), a widely used instrument for the evaluation of sleep quality, was administered to participating patients. Linear regression analyses with the PSQI as the dependent variable were computed to examine the effect of relevant demographic, lifestyle, and clinical variables on sleep quality. Impaired subjective sleep quality, as assessed by the PSQI, was observed in approximately half of the patients. Low sleep quality was independently associated with age, anxiety and depressive symptoms, and pain associated with dystonia, whereas no association emerged between sleep quality and variables related to the motor manifestations of dystonia, or lifestyle variables. Impaired sleep quality is common in patients with IAOD and appears to be more strongly associated with age, pain, and psychiatric symptoms than with several parameters related to motor manifestations. Thus, sleep disturbances in IAOD may be largely correlated to coexisting non-motor features.
