papers.title: Artificial intelligence in epilepsy care: a systematic review and meta-analysis of clinical applications in diagnosis, classification, outcome prediction, and surgical decision-making.
papers.abstract: Epilepsy affects approximately 50 million people worldwide, with disproportionate burden in low- and middle-income countries where access to specialized care remains limited. Despite advances in neuroimaging and electrophysiology, accurate diagnosis, etiological classification, and timely identification of surgical candidates remain major clinical challenges. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool to integrate multimodal data and support clinical decision-making across the epilepsy care continuum. To systematically assess and meta-analytically quantify the evidence on AI applications for diagnosis, etiological classification, outcome prediction, surgical candidate selection, and workflow optimization in epilepsy. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, with protocol registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251117939). Searches were performed in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, Cochrane Library, and SciELO for studies published between January 2014 and March 2026. Eligible studies included original research in human subjects with epilepsy applying AI or machine learning models and reporting at least one quantitative performance metric with internal or external validation. Study quality was assessed using PROBAST. Pooled estimates of Area Under the Curve (AUC), sensitivity, and specificity were derived using DerSimonian-Laird random-effects models across four clinical task groups: diagnosis, classification, outcome prediction, and surgical referral. From 423 identified records, 102 studies met inclusion criteria. Research output increased markedly after 2018, peaking in 2021 and 2024, with geographic concentration in China (n = 31) and the United States (n = 11). Electroencephalography and MRI were the dominant input modalities, and Support Vector Machines (n = 41) and Convolutional Neural Networks (n = 22) were the most frequently employed algorithms. Most studies relied exclusively on internal validation, and external validation remained scarce across all domains. PROBAST assessment revealed high risk of bias in the majority of studies, particularly in the participant and analysis domains. Meta-analysis demonstrated strong discriminative performance across all groups: the classification group achieved the highest pooled AUC (0.929; 95% CI: 0.837-0.971), followed by diagnosis (0.899; 95% CI: 0.859-0.929), surgical referral (0.895; 95% CI: 0.870-0.916), and outcome prediction (0.807; 95% CI: 0.740-0.861). Sensitivity was highest in the diagnosis group (0.885; 95% CI: 0.840-0.918) and lowest in surgical referral (0.729; 95% CI: 0.681-0.771), a clinically relevant asymmetry given the high cost of missing true surgical candidates in drug-resistant epilepsy. Substantial variability was observed across studies, reflecting differences in data modalities, AI architectures, and sample sizes, and indicating that pooled estimates should be interpreted with caution rather than as fixed, generalizable performance figures. AI demonstrates robust and clinically meaningful performance across the spectrum of epilepsy care, particularly for diagnosis and surgical planning. However, uniformly high between-study heterogeneity, predominant reliance on internal validation, variable study quality, and underrepresentation of low- and middle-income country contexts limit the generalizability of current evidence and hinder clinical translation. Prospective multicenter studies, standardized reporting, and context-adapted implementation strategies are essential to realize the full clinical potential that this body of evidence consistently demonstrates.

papers.title: Mechanism of the lysosomal calcium signaling TRPML1-TFEB axis in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a prevalent chronic neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive apoptosis of midbrain substantia nigra dopaminergic neurons, striatal dopamine depletion, and α-synuclein (α-syn)-positive Lewy-body formation. Patients exhibit motor deficits (resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability) plus non-motor manifestations such as cognitive and sleep impairment. PD pathogenesis arises from intertwined mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, defective protein degradation and disrupted calcium homeostasis, whose precise mechanisms remain incompletely defined. As both a degradative organelle and signaling hub, lysosomes govern clearance of proteins and damaged organelles and mediate key neuronal events through calcium-dependent signaling. Transient Receptor Potential Mucolipin 1 (TRPML1), a lysosomal calcium-release channel, and Transcription Factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosome biogenesis and autophagic flux, constitute the conserved TRPML1-TFEB axis that couples lysosomal calcium signaling to transcriptional control of cellular degradation. Physiologically, TRPML1-triggered calcium release activates calcineurin to drive TFEB dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation, one of several convergent routes that maintain neuronal protein and organelle homeostasis; TFEB is likewise engaged by the second lysosomal calcium channel TPC2, by mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) inhibition and by oxidative-stress-dependent phosphatases. Pathological TRPML1 malfunction perturbs lysosomal calcium signaling and suppresses TFEB activity, triggering lysosomal defects, autophagic blockage, α-syn buildup, mitochondrial damage and oxidative stress, which culminate in dopaminergic neuronal death and PD progression. Mounting data identify dysregulation of this axis as a core pathogenic driver bridging lysosomal failure and neurodegeneration across genetic, toxic and ageing-related PD, although for several disease genes the available evidence documents TFEB-dependent lysosomal failure without direct TRPML1 perturbation. This review summarizes this axis' molecular-physiological features, its pathological crosstalk with major PD events, targeted therapeutic progress, research limitations and future directions, offering theoretical clues for PD mechanistic study and novel therapeutic development.

papers.title: [Beyond the ECG-the emotional side of electrophysiology].
Filgotinib Safety Profile: A Pharmacovigilance Study Using Data from the VigiBase and Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System.
papers.abstract: Although filgotinib was approved in Europe and Japan, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) withheld approval owing to concerns about testicular toxicity. To address this gap, we conducted a pharmacovigilance study of filgotinib-related adverse drug reactions (ADRs). This study evaluated the safety profile of filgotinib using data from the VigiBase and FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) databases from the first quarter (Q1) of 2017 to Q1 2025. Signal detection involved calculating four disproportionality measures: the proportional reporting ratio (PRR), reporting odds ratio (ROR), information component (IC), and empirical Bayes geometric mean (EBGM), using predefined quantitative thresholds. Signals were refined using OpenVigil 2.1 to account for concomitant medications. The signals were ordered according to their IC025 values rather than PRR value. Analysis of VigiBase data (2207 reports) revealed a predominance of ADRs among female patients (74.8%) and individuals aged 45-64 years (38.1%). Notably, 95% of reports originated in Europe. Strong disproportionate reporting signals were identified for lower respiratory tract infection (PRR = 20.5 [χ2 = 1002.3], lower bound [LB] ROR = 16, IC025 = 3.7, EBGM05 = 15.6) and hypercholesterolemia (PRR = 29.8 [χ2 = 611.9], LB ROR = 19.8, IC025 = 3.5, EBGM05 = 19.5). Time-to-onset analysis revealed diverse onset times (median, 1 month), with most ADRs assessed as possibly related to filgotinib. In FAERS (190 reports), disproportionate reporting signals were observed for epididymitis (PRR = 1060.3 [χ2 = 8350.6], LB ROR = 544.1, IC025 = 2.9, EBGM05 = 512.0) and sleep apnea syndrome (PRR = 62.7 [χ2 = 486.0], LB ROR = 32.3, IC025 = 2.6, EBGM05 = 30.8). This pharmacovigilance study identified several disproportionality signals, including epididymitis, sleep apnea syndrome, infections, and metabolic abnormalities, warranting continued clinical vigilance and further investigation of the safety profile of filgotinib.

papers.title: Membrane Lipid Composition and Asymmetry Modulate Translocation Versus Leakage of the Model Amphipathic Peptide MAP.
papers.abstract: Cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) can enable intracellular access while avoiding cytotoxicity, yet their behavior is highly sensitive to membrane composition. Here we show that lipid composition and leaflet asymmetry act as a switch that determines whether the amphipathic CPP MAP undergoes nondisruptive translocation or stabilizes membrane pores that drive leakage. Using high-field computational electrophysiology (CompEL) simulations in membranes of increasing physiological relevance, we show that electrically induced membrane defects allow the insertion of MAP peptides. We find symmetric anionic bilayers favor MAP insertion coupled to transmembrane pore stabilization in POPC/POPG membranes, reproducing progressive dye release in liposome leakage assays. Incorporation of cholesterol reduces the number of inserted peptides and conducts to faster leakage kinetics in cholesterol-containing vesicles. In contrast, a minimal asymmetric membrane model (POPC extracellular leaflet; POPC/POPS intracellular leaflet) supports MAP translocation without sustained membrane disruption. This delivery-relevant mechanism is supported by efficient MAP internalization in HEK293 cells while maintaining high viability. Polarized ATR-FTIR provides structural context, indicating predominantly membrane-associated α-helical conformations across lipid compositions. Together, these results establish lipid asymmetry and composition as actionable biointerface parameters that tune CPP function between translocation and leakage and demonstrate an experimentally benchmarked framework for predicting membrane outcomes across complex lipid environments.

papers.title: When Screens Intervene: The Mediating Role of Evening Screen Use in Adolescent Mental Health and Sleep via Temporal Analyses.
papers.abstract: This study examined how daily mental health related to sleep and how screen use in bed might mediate these relationships. Bedtime electronic devices were an 8-day, repeated-measures, observational study. Seventy five adolescents (11-14.9 years) completed daily mental health measures (health-related quality of life [HRQoL]; KIDSCREEN-10, well-being; WHO-5, and mood) via smartphone questionnaires. Evening screen use was measured using video cameras from 2 hours before bed until sleep. Sleep onset and duration were measured using wrist-worn AX3 accelerometers and perceived sleep quality via daily morning questionnaires. Mixed-effects regression models estimated temporal associations, with and without adjustment for screen use. In this diverse sample (36% indigenous Māori), teens spent 26.6 (standard deviation 13.9) minutes on screens in the 2 hours before bed and 14.1 minutes (standard deviation 24.2) while in bed. Poorer well-being during the day was not associated with screen use prebed but was with in-bed use that evening (standardized mean difference, 95% confidence interval: -0.20; -0.33, 0.08 mood, -0.13; -0.27, -0.01 HRQoL). While HRQoL, well-being, and mood all predicted lower sleep quality, this was not mediated by screen use in bed. However, screen use in bed partially mediated relationships between poorer mood and later sleep onset (64.6% mediated) and total sleep time (39.2% mediated). Screen use in bed partly mediated relationships between daily mood and sleep quantity but not quality. This suggests that removing screens from the bedroom could act as a possible 'circuit breaker', disrupting the impact of poorer daily mood on some aspects of sleep health.

papers.title: Obstructive sleep apnea may exacerbate periodontitis via microbial dysbiosis: A preliminary translational exploratory study.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is characterized by recurrent airway obstruction and could lead to chronic intermittent hypoxia (CIH). Its relationship with periodontitis and underlying biological mechanisms, however, remains unclear. This translational human observation and experimental animal study aims (1) to investigate whether OSA exacerbates periodontitis and (2) to explore potential microbial and metabolic mechanisms. In the clinical component, patients with stage II periodontitis were allocated into two groups: periodontitis without OSA (N-OSA + P) and periodontitis with OSA (OSA + P). Gingival crevicular fluid (GCF) was analyzed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics. In the experimental study, eight male Wistar rats with ligature-induced periodontitis (P) were randomly assigned to normoxia or CIH exposure. Micro-CT, histological staining, ELISA, and qRT-PCR were performed to assess alveolar bone loss and inflammation responses. Demographic parameters were comparable between clinical groups. The OSA + P group exhibited higher microbial richness and a distinct subgingival community structure, characterized by enrichment of Porphyromonas gingivalis and Fusobacterium. 21 endogenous differential metabolites were identified, primarily related to glycerophospholipid metabolism, with significant microbe-metabolite correlations observed. In the animal model, CIH exposure was associated with increased alveolar bone loss, enhanced inflammatory marker expression, and altered microbial community structure compared with normoxic controls. The presence of sleep breathing disturbances, such as OSA, seems to exacerbate periodontitis most likely by CIH, which leads to microbial dysbiosis, and metabolic reprogramming within the periodontal microenvironment.

papers.title: Direct cortical electrical stimulation-induced seizures: Are they reliable? A systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: We aimed to assess the frequency, clinical relevance, and prognostic value of stimulation-induced seizures (SIS) during intracranial EEG recording (iEEG), and to compare high-frequency (HF) and low-frequency (LF) stimulation protocols. We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies reporting SIS during preoperative iEEG. Pooled proportions of SIS and habitual seizures were estimated using random-effects models. Differences between HF and LF stimulation were assessed using odds ratios. Study-level meta-regression was conducted to evaluate associations between SIS rates, habitual seizure proportions, and postoperative favorable seizure outcome (Engel Ia). Twenty-five studies were included. SIS occurred more frequently with HF than LF stimulation (56.1% vs. 35.8%; OR 1.83, 95% CI 1.50-2.23; p < 0.001), with substantial between-study heterogeneity. Among patients with SIS, LF stimulation was associated with a higher proportion of habitual seizures compared to HF (81.8% vs. 72.9%), although this difference was not statistically significant. A higher proportion of habitual electro-clinical seizures among SIS correlated with increased rates of favorable seizure outcomes with LF stimulation (p = 0.004) but not with HF stimulation (p = 0,912). Finally, MRI-visible lesions and the mesio-temporal seizure-onset zone were associated with higher SIS rates (p < 0.01). In conclusion, HF stimulation increases the likelihood of inducing SIS, but SIS frequency was not associated with a higher proportion of favorable seizure outcomes. Instead, the clinical relevance of SIS depends on their similarity to habitual seizures. These findings suggest that SIS may reflect underlying network excitability, and that their diagnostic value lies in their semiological and EEG concordance rather than occurrence of stimulated seizures alone. Overall, these results emphasize the importance of stimulation-induced habitual electro-clinical seizures for postsurgical outcome prognostication.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence-enabled quality assurance for point-of-care electroencephalographic cap placement by inexperienced users.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) remains inaccessible in many health care settings, including low- and middle-income countries and point-of-care environments where trained EEG technologists are unavailable. Although low-cost EEG systems enable inexperienced users to acquire EEG, reliable acquisition also requires quality assurance of accurate electrode array positioning. We developed an artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled tool to address this need. We conducted a prospective randomized crossover validation study comparing AI-guided EEG cap fitting by inexperienced users with placement by an expert EEG technologist. A blinded expert quantified positioning error against International 10-20 System targets and independently rated overall placement as optimal, usable, or incorrect. Thirty participants completed 60 placement trials. Mean absolute positioning error was .938 cm with app-guided and .855 cm with expert placement. The mean paired difference was .084 cm (90% confidence interval = .024-.143), demonstrating noninferiority against the prespecified .5-cm margin. Clinically acceptable placement (optimal or usable) was achieved in 28 of 30 (93.3%) app-guided and 30 of 30 (100%) expert trials. AI-enabled quality assurance enabled inexperienced users to achieve electrode array positioning noninferior to expert placement, supporting its potential use in expanding access to point-of-care EEG.

papers.title: Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation for fibromyalgia: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Fibromyalgia is a chronic pain syndrome associated with central sensitization, autonomic dysfunction, and neuroimmune dysregulation. Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) has emerged as a promising non-pharmacological neuromodulatory intervention targeting pain processing, autonomic balance, and inflammatory pathways. However, evidence regarding its efficacy in fibromyalgia remains limited. To systematically evaluate the efficacy, safety, and potential clinical implications of taVNS in patients with fibromyalgia through qualitative synthesis and meta-analysis. A systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library were searched for studies evaluating taVNS in fibromyalgia. Primary outcomes included pain reduction, while secondary outcomes comprised functional status, sleep quality, psychological symptoms, autonomic parameters, and safety. Random-effects meta-analysis estimated standardized within-group changes in pain rather than comparative between-group treatment effects. Five studies involving 333 patients fulfilled eligibility criteria and were included in the qualitative synthesis. Three studies comprising 100 patients contributed to the quantitative analysis. Meta-analysis demonstrated a large standardized within-group improvement in pain following taVNS-based interventions (Hedges g = 2.75; 95% CI 1.38-4.11). However, substantial between-study heterogeneity (I² = 91.4%) and the limited number of studies warrant cautious interpretation. Across studies, taVNS-based interventions were associated with improvements in pain intensity, Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire scores, anxiety symptoms, sleep quality, and overall disease burden. Akkurt et al. additionally reported improvements in autonomic parameters. Considerable variability existed in stimulation protocols, treatment duration, comparator groups, and concomitant interventions. Some studies combined taVNS with exercise therapy or pain neuroscience education, limiting attribution of benefits specifically to vagal stimulation. Reported adverse effects were mild, and treatment tolerability was generally favorable. Current evidence suggests that taVNS may provide clinical benefits for patients with fibromyalgia, particularly regarding pain, functional status, psychological symptoms, sleep quality, and autonomic regulation. Nevertheless, small sample sizes, substantial methodological and statistical heterogeneity, concomitant interventions, and limited follow-up preclude definitive conclusions regarding efficacy. Larger, adequately powered, sham-controlled randomized trials employing standardized stimulation protocols and clinically meaningful outcomes are necessary to establish the therapeutic effectiveness of taVNS in fibromyalgia.

papers.title: "Howzat!" sleep patterns, nocturnal physiology, and performance in professional cricket umpires during a Twenty20 cricket tournament.
papers.abstract: We aimed to characterise sleep behaviour and nocturnal physiological responses in 15 professional cricket umpires (13 male, 2 female; age 45 ± 8 y) across a 6-week Australian Twenty20 cricket tournament using smart rings. Linear mixed-effects models compared sleep outcomes between match and non-match nights, home vs. away matches, and officiating roles (on-field vs. TV). Associations were assessed between night-before sleep and officiating performance. Sleep duration was lower following match than non-match nights (5 h 52 min vs. 7 h 54 min, p < 0.05), alongside later bedtimes, reduced time in bed, and delayed sleep midpoint. Nocturnal heart rate was higher and heart rate variability was lower on match than non-match nights without differences in sleep efficiency between conditions. Later estimated match finish was associated with less sleep (p < 0.05). Home matches were associated with earlier bedtimes and longer sleep, while TV umpires obtained more sleep and showed higher sleep efficiency (+3.8%) than on-field umpires (all p < 0.05). No associations were observed between night-before sleep and officiating performance in either role, after multiple-comparison correction. These findings highlight how competition scheduling affects sleep in cricket umpires and the need to optimise scheduling and consider sleep support strategies during tournaments.

papers.title: Affective responses during five days of dexmedetomidine-assisted cold-sleep for long-duration spaceflight.
papers.abstract: Quasi-torpor, known as "cold-sleep," is an inducible state of metabolic suppression and mild hypothermia proposed to reduce resource demands and psychological stress during long-duration spaceflight. While cold-sleep can reduce metabolic rate, its psychological effects remain unknown. We tested whether affective valence and arousal measured with the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS) varied during a five-day dexmedetomidine-assisted cold-sleep protocol, hypothesizing decreased arousal and unchanged valence. We enrolled six healthy volunteers (5 male, 1 female). Five received the cold-sleep intervention, and one served as a control. Participants received an oral dexmedetomidine loading dose followed by an 18-hour subcutaneous infusion with external cooling, then approximately 2 hours of sleep and subsequent cognitive and exercise testing. PANAS was administered daily at hour 23. Positive Affect (PA), Negative Affect (NA), valence (PA-NA), and arousal (PA+NA) were assessed using mixed-effects modeling including the early-withdrawal participant (n = 5). Four participants completed all five days, and one withdrew after Day 3 for reasons unrelated to the study. Mixed-effects modeling showed no significant day effect for valence or arousal (both p = 0.27). PA and NA showed no day-related trends. Two participants completed recovery PANAS assessments, which were equivalent to Day 5. The placebo control qualitatively showed a similar pattern. Across five days of dexmedetomidine-assisted cold-sleep, participants showed no major adverse affective outcome or recovery rebound. These findings support continued evaluation of metabolic suppression strategies for long-duration spaceflight.

papers.title: Sleep and Mood in Retinitis Pigmentosa.
papers.abstract: The purpose of this study was to identify whether retinitis pigmentosa (RP) has an impact on sleep and mood, and whether disease severity exacerbates this. Eighty-seven patients with an RP phenotype of inherited retinal dystrophy were recruited from Oxford University Hospital NHS Trust. Three hundred three healthy controls were also recruited from the participating centers. Subjective sleep quality was assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). Anxiety and depression (e.g. "mood") was quantified using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) and daytime sleepiness using the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS). Mann-Whitney U testing was used for between-group statistical comparisons. Spearman's rho coefficient was used to explore correlations between factors. Individuals with RP had significantly worse global sleep quality (PSQI; P = 0.0375) compared with controls. This was due primarily to altered sleep efficiency (P = 0.0034). Regression analyses of participants with RP suggest the driver for poorer sleep was visual acuity (P = 0.0197), particularly in sleep duration (P = 0.0066). Poor visual acuity significantly correlated with poor rod and cone responses and loss of visual field. However, only decreased visual acuity was significant for poorer sleep. Across all groups, increased PSQI (e.g. worsened sleep) correlated with significantly worsened HADS (r = 0.2755, P < 0.0001). HADS scores were not significantly increased in RP participants versus controls. Our study identified poorer sleep in patients with RP, which correlated with reduced visual acuity. Levels of anxiety and depression were similar between groups.

papers.title: Liraglutide Realigns Corneal Circadian Output Programs and Ameliorates Ocular Surface Abnormalities Under High-Fat-Diet-Induced Metabolic Stress.
papers.abstract: High-fat diet (HFD)-induced metabolic dysfunction is associated with ocular surface disease, but its effects on corneal circadian organization remain unclear. We investigated HFD-associated corneal circadian remodeling and its modification by liraglutide. Male C57BL/6J mice received normal chow (NC), HFD, or HFD plus liraglutide during an eight-week protocol; liraglutide was administered during the final four weeks. Corneas collected at eight Zeitgeber time points over 24 hours underwent bulk RNA sequencing, rhythmicity, differential-rhythmicity, phase-set, and network analyses. Ocular-surface epithelial, immune, neural, and structural phenotypes were also assessed. HFD increased rhythmic transcripts from 2040 to 3582, delayed mean peak phase from ZT0:46 to ZT7:47, and reduced phase coherence from r = 0.33 to 0.13. In HFD+LIRA corneas, these measures shifted toward NC (2640 transcripts, ZT0:18, r = 0.31). Among 10 examined canonical core-clock genes, only one met the defined significant phase-shift criterion in HFD versus NC, and amplitude distributions did not differ significantly among groups. Liraglutide treatment was also associated with increased epithelial ZO-1 and Occludin signals, greater corneal nerve fiber density, improved mechanical sensitivity, and reduced neutrophil and γδ T-cell accumulation versus HFD alone. HFD broadly remodels corneal circadian output organization while the examined canonical core-clock parameters show comparatively limited changes. Liraglutide shifts multiple temporal features toward the NC pattern and is associated with improved epithelial, immune, neural, and structural ocular-surface phenotypes.

papers.title: Agreement between actigraphy and sleep diary during the perinatal period.
papers.abstract: Wearable devices are increasingly used in nursing research, with actigraphy being commonly used for sleep assessment. This study aimed to evaluate the agreement between actigraphy and sleep diary during the perinatal period and examine whether the agreement would change by phase and based on symptom severity (fatigue, depression, and insomnia). This secondary analysis used data from a prospective cohort. Data were collected at early, mid-, late pregnancy and 6-month postpartum. Participants completed 1-week sleep diary and wore Actiwatch at each time. Bland-Altman analyses evaluated the agreement for sleep measures, with mean differences defined as actigraphy minus sleep diary. Linear mixed-effects models examined phase and symptom related changes in mean difference. Sensitivity analyses were performed. The analytic sample across the four phases were 64, 66, 67, and 54, respectively. Mean differences ranged from 4.6 to 14.1 min for total sleep time (TST), 5.9 to 8.2% for sleep efficiency (SE), -3.2 to 0.3 min for sleep onset latency, and 4.8 to 13.7 min for wake after sleep onset. Mean differences were within the recommended a priori clinical significance thresholds, except for SE. Limits of agreement were generally wide, and all were beyond these thresholds. No significant phase or symptom severity effects on mean differences were detected, except for fatigue. In conclusion, agreement was good at group level (except for SE), but poor at individual level. Agreement remained largely stable across phases and symptom severities. Concurrent use of both methods is recommended in nursing research among pregnant women, wherever feasible.

papers.title: JAK Inhibition in Febrile Infection-Related Epilepsy Syndrome: A Case Series from Sydney Children's Hospital.
papers.abstract: Febrile Infection-Related Epilepsy Syndrome (FIRES) is a subcategory of New-Onset Refractory Status Epilepticus (NORSE) occurring in previously healthy individuals following a mild febrile illness. FIRES is a challenging paediatric condition with a mortality of 12% and permanent neurocognitive deficits in up to 90% of survivors. Pathogenesis appears to involve innate immune dysregulation, and first-line immunotherapy (intravenous immunoglobulin [IVIG], corticosteroids) is ineffective in most cases. A number of second-line cytokine-directed therapies have been trialled in individual case reports and short case series, but with similarly unencouraging outcomes. We describe three paediatric patients managed at Sydney Children's Hospital between 2024 and 2026 in whom baricitinib, a JAK1/2 inhibitor, was incorporated into the immunotherapy regimen for FIRES. Patient 1 was a 13-year-old girl diagnosed with FIRES with refractory status epilepticus. After 2 months of uncontrolled seizures with profound functional decline and brain atrophy, baricitinib was added to her treatment regimen. While she eventually succumbed to her illness, the introduction of JAK inhibition was accompanied by electroencephalogram (EEG) normalisation within two weeks. Patient 2, a 15-year-old girl, presented following a post-appendicectomy febrile illness. She developed refractory status epilepticus with negative autoimmune and paraneoplastic workup and markedly elevated neopterin (347 nmol/L; normal range [NR] = 0 - 30). Treatment with IVIG, methylprednisolone, and plasma exchange (PLEX) followed by baricitinib and anakinra achieved seizure control over a period of weeks. Intermittent focal seizures and encephalopathic EEG changes persist, but with return to premorbid function and return to school. Patient 3 is a 16-year-old girl who presented in March 2026 with febrile encephalopathy and escalating seizures. Following intubation, multi-agent antiepileptic therapy, and immunosuppression, including baricitinib, anakinra, and IVIG, she was extubated after 2 weeks with subsequent functional recovery, returning to school with mild residual cognitive and emotional changes. This case series adds to the limited evidence supporting early and aggressive JAK inhibition in paediatric FIRES. The addition of baricitinib appears to offer clinically meaningful seizure reduction and EEG improvement when used alongside cytokine-directed therapy.

papers.title: Emergence of ANTI-GAD65 Autoimmunity in Longstanding Drug-Resistant Temporal Lobe Epilepsy.
papers.abstract: Glutamic acid decarboxylase 65 autoantibodies (anti-GAD65 Abs) are associated with a spectrum of neurological syndromes, including chronic temporal lobe epilepsy. Although immunosuppressive therapy is generally considered less effective in long-standing anti-GAD65-associated epilepsy, emerging evidence suggests that selected patients may derive a meaningful benefit. We present a patient with longstanding drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy, in whom high-titre serum anti-GAD65 Abs were identified during evaluation for epilepsy surgery, with subsequent marked improvement in seizure burden following treatment with corticosteroids, immunoglobulin, rituximab, and mycophenolate mofetil. We report a 29-year-old female with a history of temporal lobe epilepsy, initially diagnosed in 2014, presenting with headaches, short-term memory loss, and focal seizures. In 2015, the patient re-presented with altered mental state and increased seizure frequency, with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) testing confirming herpes simplex virus encephalitis. Serum anti-GAD65 Ab testing was negative. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated left temporal encephalomalacia. The persistent burden of refractory focal seizures to anti-epileptic therapy in the subsequent years led to the recent consideration of epilepsy surgery. Detection of high-titre serum anti-GAD65 Abs during the workup raised concerns for a diagnosis of autoimmune epilepsy, with anti-GAD65 Abs also detected in CSF. Pre-treatment video electroencephalogram (EEG) demonstrated significant seizure burden from the right temporal region with 68 focal seizures in the first 44 hours of evaluation. Treatment was instigated with methylprednisolone, followed by intravenous immunoglobulin. Rituximab induction was then implemented, along with mycophenolate mofetil and a weaning dose of oral prednisolone. A 24-hour EEG was repeated, which demonstrated one single brief subclinical seizure, representing a marked reduction in seizure burden. Ongoing clinical and electrophysiological follow-up is underway. This case adds to the limited evidence supporting intensive immunosuppressive treatment in selected patients with anti-GAD65-associated chronic epilepsy. It further highlights the potential value of repeat anti-GAD65 Abs testing in patients with longstanding drug-resistant epilepsy with clinical suspicion for autoimmune temporal lobe epilepsy.

papers.title: Self-reported sleep problems and associated factors among older adults in Malaysia: An ethnic subgroup analysis.
papers.abstract: This study examines factors associated with self-reported sleep problems within a large sample of older Malaysian adults from diverse ethnic groups. Cross-sectional data from the South East Asia Community Observatory Health Survey 2018 and ordered probit models were used for analysis. Malay females were more likely to report mild-to-severe sleep problems than males. Malays and Chinese who were older were more likely to report mild-to-severe sleep problems compared to younger ones. Among Malays, smoking was associated with the likelihood of reporting mild-to-severe sleep problems. Higher income, physically active and obese older Chinese adults were less likely to report sleep problems than others. Being diagnosed with hypertension among Chinese and diabetes among Indians was associated with a higher probability of reporting mild-to-severe sleep problems. Sociodemographic characteristics, lifestyles and health profiles are key factors associated with self-reported sleep problems among various ethnic groups of Malaysian older adults.

papers.title: Sleep Regularity in Young Adults With and Without Unmanaged Sleep Disorders.
papers.abstract: Irregular sleep is associated with negative health and performance outcomes, including cardiovascular disease and impaired attentional performance. Young adults with unmanaged sleep disorders may be particularly vulnerable to health and safety risks associated with irregular sleep, but sleep regularity in this group is not yet well-characterized. This study describes sleep regularity in young adults with unmanaged sleep disorders relative to healthy sleepers. Seventy-two young adults (60% female; Age [mean ± SD] = 25.1 ± 4.6 years) recorded sleep-wake patterns using daily diaries over 7-21 days. Sleep disorder diagnoses were confirmed by trained clinicians using the Structured Clinical Interview for Sleep Disorders (Revised; SCISD-R), diagnostic polysomnography and validated questionnaires (e.g., Insomnia Severity Index, Epworth Sleepiness Scale). Sleep regularity was quantified using the Sleep Regularity Index (SRI). Bootstrapped regressions were used to compare SRI between sleep disorder types and healthy sleepers. Of the sleep disorder groups examined, only individuals with Delayed Sleep-Wake Phase Disorder (DSWPD) exhibited significantly lower SRI (Median SRI (IQR): 75.8(66.6-80.7)) than healthy sleepers (79.4(76.0-85.0)), B = -8.4, 95% CI[-15.5, -2.1]. There was a trend towards lower SRI in individuals presenting with DSWPD comorbid with Obstructive Sleep Apnea (72.2(66.0-78.2)), B = -10.5[-25.0, 2.1]; and Insomnia (78.2(69.7-81.1)), B = -3.6[-8.9 to 2.0]. Lower sleep regularity in young adults with DSWPD likely reflects a misalignment between biological sleep timing and external obligations (e.g., early morning commitments). Regularizing sleep-wake timing may be a worthwhile target in DSWPD treatment. Further research is warranted to consider the effect of targeted sleep regularity interventions in this population alongside existing treatment recommendations. papers.title: Automated Home-Cage Sipper Devices Reveal Age and Sex Differences in Ethanol Consumption Patterns.
papers.abstract: Alcohol consumption and alcohol use disorder (AUD) are influenced by circadian rhythms, which differ with age and sex. Little research has compared circadian ethanol consumption patterns across ages and sexes. Cost-effective, open-source Arduino-based home-cage sipper devices could elucidate these patterns. We hypothesized these devices would reveal phase and/or amplitude changes in circadian drinking rhythms in ethanol-drinking mice that would vary by age and sex. We used Arduino-based home-cage sipper devices in continuous-access two-bottle choice (2 bc) with water and ethanol (10% v/v) for 14 days to measure drinking patterns of male and female adolescent (3-week), young adult (6-week), and mature adult (18-week) C57BL/6J mice. Grams per kilogram (g/kg) fluid consumption was manually recorded at the beginning of each dark cycle, while sipper devices continuously recorded drinking. Manually collected 2 bc data confirmed greater ethanol consumption in females and stepwise decreases in total fluid consumption with age in ethanol-drinking females and in both sexes in the water-only groups. Correlations of manually recorded versus sipper count data were strong and significant for ethanol, but weaker for water. Blood ethanol concentrations significantly correlated with sipper data, indicating sipper devices can determine temporal ethanol consumption. Sipper devices uncovered subtle differences in circadian rhythms by age, group, and ethanol consumption, including minor phase advancement with ethanol consumption with age in females, but delay in males, as well as a female-specific phase delay and weaker amplitude in total fluid consumption across age groups with ethanol consumption. We show these devices capture circadian patterns of drinking behavior differing by age, sex, and ethanol consumption inaccessible by manual 2 bc measurements. Future studies may examine older age groups and further dissect circadian drinking patterns by age and sex and their molecular mechanisms relevant to AUD pathogenesis.

papers.title: Association of Dietary Quality and Working Hours With Sleep Health in US Adults: Evidence From National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 2007-2014.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to assess the respective associations of dietary quality and working hours with insufficient sleep and sleep disorders among US adults and to examine the associations of combined work-diet patterns. In this cross-sectional study, data were obtained from the 2007-2014 NHANES. Dietary quality was assessed using the Healthy Eating Index 2015 (HEI-2015), and working hours were measured based on self-reported weekly working hours. Four work-diet patterns were created according to dietary quality and working hours. Insufficient sleep was defined as a sleep duration of ≤ 6 h, and sleep disorders were self-reported by respondents. Weighted logistic regression was used as the primary analysis. Among the 8339 respondents, 41.1% experienced insufficient sleep and 6.9% reported sleep disorders. In the fully adjusted model, higher dietary quality was not significantly associated with insufficient sleep (OR: 0.834, 95% CI: 0.693-1.005) or sleep disorders (OR: 0.716, 95% CI: 0.506-1.014). Shorter working hours were associated with lower odds of insufficient sleep (OR: 0.828, 95% CI: 0.720-0.952), but not sleep disorders (OR: 0.848, 95% CI: 0.661-1.088). Regarding the combined work-diet patterns, individuals with a healthy diet and shorter working hours had significantly lower odds of insufficient sleep (OR: 0.697, 95% CI: 0.568-0.854) and sleep disorders (OR: 0.623, 95% CI: 0.439-0.882) after adjustment for potential confounders. In this nationally representative study, a healthy diet and shorter working hours were associated with lower odds of insufficient sleep and sleep disorders. Maintaining healthy dietary habits together with reasonable working hours may be associated with better sleep health.

papers.title: Implementing a Comprehensive Patient-Reported Outcome Framework for Chronic Urticaria in Clinical Practice.
papers.abstract: Chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) is a burdensome inflammatory skin condition that substantially impairs health-related quality of life and is frequently accompanied by sleep disturbances and psychiatric comorbidities such as anxiety and depression. While international guidelines advocate continuous assessment with patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), clinical inertia and time constraints limit their real-world implementation. To propose a practical, two-level framework that guides integrating PROMs into routine clinical practice. Narrative review informed by the expertise of members of Urticaria Centers of Reference and Excellence (UCARE), based on searches of PubMed, Web of Science and Scopus (last 10 years) and the 2026 international guideline. The core set, applied to all patients with CSU at every visit, comprises the UAS7 (disease activity), the UCT (disease control) and the CU-Q2oL (quality of life). Second-level assessments are added according to clinical need: angioedema-specific instruments (AAS, AECT, AE-QoL), instruments for chronic inducible urticarias, and brief screening tools for mental health and sleep (e.g., PHQ-4, PHQ-9, GAD-7, ISI) in patients with poorly controlled disease, high quality-of-life impact or a suggestive history. Digital platforms such as the CRUSE application can support data collection alongside paper diaries. This framework may help clinicians detect uncontrolled disease and often overlooked comorbidities and align management with international guidelines. Its feasibility and impact require prospective evaluation.

papers.title: How Perceived Traits Modulate the Neural Processing of Reward During Reinforcement Learning.
papers.abstract: Humans infer others' traits through positive and negative feedback, and these perceived traits, in turn, shape how individuals perceive others' behavior. Although previous studies have investigated the neural basis of reward and trait learning, the temporal dynamics by which trait-level learning signals modulate reward-related brain responses during learning remain poorly understood. In this study, we used reinforcement learning models to separate participants' processing of reward and generosity prediction errors (PEs), and used EEG to examine how perceived traits modulate the neural processing of reward. Behavioral analyses indicated that both reward and perceived generosity influenced decision making during the learning phase. In the test phase, perceived trait information played a more significant role in guiding decisions. Neurally, positive reward PEs elicited larger reward positivity amplitudes, stronger delta power, and reduced N400 amplitudes compared to negative reward PEs only when generosity PEs were negative. This pattern may reflect an increased focus on reward outcomes when experienced generosity is less than expected during the learning phase. These results elucidate how trait learning asymmetrically modulates reward salience and evaluation, a mechanism that may promote the prioritization of social knowledge in future choices.

papers.title: Treadmill Walking Differentially Modulates Early Auditory Responses to Standard and Deviant Sounds.
papers.abstract: People often encounter environmental sounds while walking without attending to them, but it is unclear whether walking alters early cortical responses to these sounds. We recorded 32-channel electroencephalography from 22 healthy young adults during a passive auditory frequency-oddball paradigm. Conditions were sitting and treadmill walking without an object, with a water-filled cup or with a clay-filled cup matched for mass and apparent fill height. The four conditions were compared in two pairs: sitting versus walking without carrying, and water versus clay carrying. In each comparison, we examined standard- and deviant-evoked responses in the N1 window and amplitude in the mismatch-negativity window. The sitting versus walking-without-carrying comparison showed a significant stimulus-type by movement-condition interaction 80-130 ms after sound onset. In separate, unadjusted comparisons of sitting and walking for each stimulus type, the deviant-evoked response was attenuated during walking, whereas the standard-evoked response did not differ significantly between conditions. Sensitivity analyses in the same participants yielded a smaller interaction estimate with the lowest high-pass cutoff, but filter-setting differences were unclear. In the comparison of water and clay carrying, the conditions differed kinematically, but no additional modulation of the measured auditory responses was detected. The comparison of sitting and treadmill walking showed that walking-related changes in early auditory responses differed between standard and deviant sounds. However, the contributions of frequency, probability and adaptation to this response difference could not be separated.

papers.title: Twenty-One Years of Bariatric Surgery in Benin Republic: Evolution of Techniques and Outcomes.
papers.abstract: Bariatric surgery was introduced in the Republic of Benin in 2005, yet, as in many sub-Saharan African countries, it has remained almost entirely undocumented. To describe how bariatric surgical techniques and their outcomes have evolved in Benin over a 21-year-period. Retrospective cohort study including all patients who underwent bariatric surgery between January 1, 2005, and January 31, 2026, at two hospitals in Cotonou, Benin. A total of 111 patients were included (mean age, 43.3 years; women, 85.6%; mean body mass index, 43.2 kg/m2). The procedures performed were laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (50.5%), adjustable gastric banding (37.8%), open sleeve gastrectomy (10.8%), and gastric bipartition (.9%). Gastric banding was discontinued in 2011, and laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy has been the standard procedure since 2012. Excess weight loss at 48 months was 50% after sleeve gastrectomy versus 21% after gastric banding. At 48 months, sleep apnea, hypertension, and diabetes persisted in 8%, 11%, and 12% of patients after sleeve gastrectomy, compared with 35%, 36%, and 40% after gastric banding. Morbidity and mortality rates were 6.3% and 1.8%, respectively. Bariatric surgery in Benin has successfully shifted to a minimally invasive approach, but its volume remains very low.
